new_statements.quote: Finally, I agree with both Rischel and Massenet that the pitch phenomenon here discussed is independent of "stress", which nowhere seems to form part of the Inuit prosodic system. It is true that a limited degree of extra stress may be utilised for discursive contrastive effect in some varieties and at least one dialect, Polar Eskimo, exploits this possibility to the point of applying "expressive stress" to a high percentage of utterances [...]. I take it that the coincidence of a nuclear pitch-peak and a heavy syllable (closed or long) produces the auditory impression of "stress" in most varieties.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No word stress in any Inuit dialect, Western Canadian ones (Copper = Inuinnaqtun, Sigliq = Siglitun, Netsilik) included; prosody consists of phrase/sentence-final pitch contours. In Copper (syllable-based system) the declarative fall is on the penultimate syllable and the yes/no fall on the final syllable; Sigliq marks yes/no questions by higher pitch on the syllable before the fall. Any impression of stress arises where the nuclear pitch peak lands on a heavy (closed or long-vowel) syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: A limited degree of extra stress may be used for contrastive/discursive emphasis in some varieties; Polar Eskimo (Greenland, not west2618) has frequent 'expressive stress'. Heavy syllables under the pitch peak sound stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the prosodic system generally; the contours described are sentence-final (phonological phrase / utterance), based on auditory analysis of tape recordings of one or a few speakers per area plus Fortescue's own fieldwork centred on Coppermine.
new_statements.identity_note: Fortescue's statement is pan-Inuit but his survey explicitly includes the west2618 dialects: 'Copper' (Coppermine/Kugluktuk = Inuinnaqtun, copp1244; his own fieldwork site), 'Sigliq' (Tuktoyaktuk = Siglitun, sigl1242) and Netsilik (nets1241) forms; Rankin Inlet also appears but is Kivalliq (Glottolog puts it under east2534). The Lowe 1985 grammars and Kudlak & Compton 2018 describe Siglitun and Kangiryuarmiutun (Ulukhaktok Inuinnaqtun) respectively and are silent on stress.

sources.citation: Arnhold, Anja, Emily Elfner & Richard Compton. 2023. Inuktitut and the concept of word-level prominence. In Bogomolets & van der Hulst (eds.), Word Prominence in Languages with Complex Morphologies, 138-177. OUP (authors' 2020 revision).
sources.note: South Baffin data; for other varieties reports second-hand: Fortescue 1983 concludes stress is not part of the prosodic system of any Inuit variety; 'evidence for consistent acoustic prominence has not been found for any Inuit variety investigated so far'; cites Dorais & Lowe 1982 for syllable-structure adjustments 'described under the label stress' in Siglitun.

sources.citation: Fortescue, Michael. 1983. A Comparative Manual of Affixes for the Inuit Dialects of Greenland, Canada, and Alaska. Meddelelser om Gronland, Man & Society 4.
sources.note: Western Canada dialect notes (Copper, Netsilik, Caribou, Mackenzie, pp.24-28) are segmental/morphological; only prosodic remark is Caribou 'deep falls from high level plateaus clause-finally'; 'expressive stress' is mentioned for Thule (Greenland) only. No word-stress statement for west2618 dialects.
